title: Getting older
hookLine: Seneca scolds his manager over old plane trees he planted himself, then meets an old man at the door he knew as a boy
tomorrow: a master twisted Epictetus's leg. what did Epictetus say?

cards: A favorite hoodie with frayed cuffs. A car that still starts, mostly. Seneca visits his country house and finds it crumbling.
He scolds the manager about the plane trees: gnarled, dry, hardly a leaf. Not my fault, says the manager; the trees are just old.
And Seneca, writing to his friend, admits, just between the two of them: "I had planted those trees myself."

teach.b: Then it gets funnier. At the door sits a frail old man, and Seneca asks who this broken-down old fellow is. The man answers: don't you know me?
I'm Felicio. You used to bring me little presents. He's the son of the old steward, the boy Seneca once spoiled.
Everything Seneca is calling old has aged right alongside him. The trees, the house, the old man at the door: they grew old together, and Seneca with them.
So he turns the joke on himself, and finds a teaching: "Let us cherish and love old age; for it is full of pleasure if one knows how to use it."

That's the Stoic view of aging: old age is good when it's used well, the way fruit, he says, is most welcome when almost over. Today's question: can getting older be good? Now a neighbor, in its own words.
Psalm 92 also looks at trees: "They shall still bring forth fruit in old age." What's shared: both look at an old tree and see something worth loving, not just loss.

The honest difference: for Seneca, a good old age comes from within, from how you use it. For the psalm, it comes from where you're rooted: "Those that be planted in the house of the LORD shall flourish."

how: Seneca's twelfth letter tells of his old plane trees and Felicio, the steward's son he knew as a boy, and urges cherishing old age. Jews and Christians pray Psalm 92, which pictures the righteous bearing fruit in old age.

o: slowly losing interest in the world as the years go by
aging alongside what you love, and finding good in it
trying to look younger than you are for as long as possible

Seneca concludes that old age is pure loss

games.q: your mom turns sixty and keeps calling herself "over the hill." what would fit both Seneca and Psalm 92?
o: the years can bear fruit; ask her what they've given her.
tell her she doesn't look a day over forty.
agree the best years are behind her, but say it kindly.
games.why: Seneca: old age is full of pleasure if you know how to use it. the psalm: they shall still bring forth fruit in old age.

practice: Look at one thing that has aged alongside you: a mug, a book, a ring, a tree outside the window, your own hand. Notice its wear honestly, the way Seneca finally looked at his trees.
Then notice what's good in it because of the years.

wordCard.voice: Getting older: aging alongside the things and people you love, and finding, with Seneca, pleasure in years well used.

orig.note: Latin: old age, the word in Seneca's letters.

carryVoice: Your line: grew old together. The trees, the old man at the door, and you. Until tomorrow.
